planting.note: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring once soil has warmed, in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; maga is the national tree of Puerto Rico and performs best in the warm, humid, frost-free conditions of the Gulf Coast's southernmost gardens.

directions: Maga is a handsome evergreen to semi-deciduous tree from Puerto Rico's moist forests, grown for its large, heart-shaped, glossy leaves and its showy, bell-shaped flowers borne singly along the branches through much of the year. Each flower opens a soft rose-to-lavender shade with a deep maroon throat in the morning and gradually darkens to a rich wine-red by the time it drops the following day, a color-shifting trait it shares with its coastal relative Thespesia populnea. It tolerates brief dry spells and light salt exposure once established, making it a good flowering shade or specimen tree for frost-free courtyards and streetscapes. Prune young trees lightly to encourage a strong branching structure, since mature specimens develop a broad, rounded canopy that benefits from room to spread.
sources: United States Forest Service International Institute of Tropical Forestry
University of Puerto Rico Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Transplant container-grown stock in spring into well-drained, limestone-based or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; this south Florida and Caribbean native understory shrub grows naturally in pinelands and hammocks and establishes readily with minimal irrigation once rooted.

directions: Everglades velvetseed is a small, multi-trunked tree or large shrub of south Florida hammocks and pinelands, distinguished from the related rough velvetseed (Guettarda scabra) by its smoother, more elliptic, glossy leaves. Clusters of small, fragrant, white tubular flowers appear through the warm months and draw bees and butterflies, followed by dark, rounded drupes that songbirds readily strip from the branches. It adapts well to the dappled light of an oak or pine hammock understory and tolerates the thin, rocky or sandy soils typical of its native range. Once established it needs little supplemental water, making it a low-maintenance choice for native pollinator plantings in the warmest coastal gardens.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation – Natives For Your Neighborhood

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this heat-loving relative of golden rain tree blooms later in the season and thrives in the long, humid summers of Gulf Coast landscapes.

directions: Chinese flame tree is a wide-spreading shade tree grown for its twice-pinnately compound foliage and its late-summer-into-fall display of upright yellow flower panicles, blooming several weeks after Koelreuteria paniculata. The true spectacle follows the flowers, when papery seed capsules flush a vivid rose-pink to salmon color, earning the tree its alternate name 'bougainvillea golden-rain tree' for the bougainvillea-like color of the pods. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor or clay soils with ease, making it a dependable, low-water shade and specimen tree across the Gulf Coast once established. Give it plenty of room to develop its broad, rounded canopy, and collect fallen seed pods where self-sowing becomes a nuisance.

planting.note: Set out container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; flamegold is widely planted as a street and shade tree in Florida and along the Texas Gulf Coast for its drought and salt tolerance once established.

directions: Flamegold is a smaller, more tender relative of golden rain tree, native to Taiwan and Fiji, grown for its dense rounded canopy of compound leaves and its early autumn show of bright yellow flower panicles, which open later in the year than those of Koelreuteria paniculata. The flowers give way to showy clusters of papery, rose-to-salmon-pink seed capsules that persist for weeks and provide strong fall color in climates too warm for traditional autumn foliage. It handles heat, drought, and coastal salt exposure well once rooted, making it a popular low-maintenance shade and parking-lot tree throughout peninsular Florida and the Gulf Coast. Because it is frost-tender, it is best reserved for zones 9 and warmer rather than used as a hardy landscape tree further north.

planting.note: Plant in early spring in deep, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in a site sheltered from harsh wind; softwood cuttings taken in summer root readily under mist propagation, and fresh seed can be sown in autumn in a cold frame.

directions: Yunnan dipelta is a Chinese relative of Dipelta floribunda, forming a somewhat smaller, loosely arching shrub valued for its spring display of fragrant, pale pink, tubular flowers marked with an orange-yellow throat at the base of each petal lobe. Flowering follows close behind the better-known Dipelta floribunda but tends to be slightly later and less profuse, with the papery, winged seed bracts providing secondary interest once the blooms fade. It prefers deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil and appreciates light shade from the hottest afternoon sun, especially in warmer parts of its hardiness range. Prune only lightly right after flowering to remove the oldest canes, since the shrub's gracefully arching form is easily spoiled by hard pruning.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this evergreen relative of common wintersweet keeps its glossy foliage year-round and is best propagated from semi-ripe cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Unlike the familiar deciduous Chimonanthus praecox, evergreen wintersweet keeps its glossy, narrow, dark-green leaves through the winter, making it a useful broadleaf evergreen screening shrub in woodland and shade gardens. Small, pale, waxy flowers open along the bare wood in winter and carry a lighter, more delicate fragrance than those of common wintersweet, best appreciated at close range near a path or doorway. It prefers humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil and benefits from the dappled shade of taller trees, where it is sheltered from harsh winter sun and drying wind. Because it is somewhat less cold-hardy than deciduous wintersweet, site it in a protected spot toward the warmer end of its range.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Flora of China (Missouri Botanical Garden / Harvard University Herbaria)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; because the species is dioecious, both male and female trees are needed nearby if fruit production on female trees is desired.

directions: Chinese corktree is a broad, round-headed shade tree closely related to the better-known Amur corktree, distinguished by its thinner, less deeply furrowed bark and leaflets that are downy on the underside. Its pinnately compound leaves cast dense summer shade, and small greenish-yellow flower clusters in late spring give way on female trees to clusters of small black drupes that persist into winter and are eaten by birds. The yellow inner bark has a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine, where it is known as huang bai, though in gardens the tree is valued chiefly as a tough, adaptable shade tree for difficult urban sites. It tolerates a range of soils and some drought once established, and develops a handsome, broadly rounded crown with age.
sources: Flora of China (Missouri Botanical Garden / Harvard University Herbaria)
Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; this Hamamelidaceae relative of Sycopsis sinensis is best grown from semi-ripe cuttings and appreciates shelter from harsh winter wind.

directions: Dunn's sycopsis is an evergreen shade shrub from the woodlands of central China, bearing broader, glossier leaves than the more commonly planted Sycopsis sinensis. In late winter, inconspicuous but intriguing flowers open along the stems, with clusters of yellow-tipped reddish stamens that resemble tiny starbursts against the dark evergreen foliage. It is grown primarily as a handsome broadleaf evergreen backdrop shrub for shaded borders and woodland gardens rather than for a showy bloom, filling a similar role to its relatives Fothergilla and Distylium. It is somewhat less cold-tolerant than Sycopsis sinensis, so it performs best toward the milder end of zone 8 and into zone 9, sited where it is sheltered from drying winter wind.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Flora of China (Missouri Botanical Garden / Harvard University Herbaria)
